title: How Film Speaks
lesson_goal: I want you to see that film has a grammar of shots and cuts, and to name three craft choices in a scene and what each one made you feel.
before_hook: Every film you love spoke to you in a language you never studied. A close up that made your chest tight. A cut that made you laugh before you knew why. That was not luck. Someone chose it. Today I want to hand you the grammar behind those choices, because once you see it, you cannot unsee it, and that is the eye every filmmaker needs.
watch_for: What does the camera show you up close, and why that thing and not something else?
When the shot changes, what changes in how you feel?
Can you point to one moment where the picture told the story with no words at all?

activity_brief: I want you to watch any one scene from any film you already like. In 5 to 7 sentences, name three choices the filmmaker made with the camera or the cut, and say what each choice made you feel. Do not summarize the plot. Talk only about the craft. For example, do not tell me the hero escaped. Tell me the low angle made the hero look powerful as he ran.
tool: None needed. This one is about training your eye, not using a tool.

rubric.criteria: Links each choice to a feeling

sections.title: Warm up: what your eyes already do
sections.body:
You already read film language every day without noticing. When a video makes you feel tense, excited, or sad, a filmmaker put that feeling there on purpose. It was a choice, not an accident.

Take five minutes. Think of one scene from any film or show that stuck with you. Do not worry yet about why. Hold it in your mind. By the end of this task you will take it apart like a maker, not just a viewer.

sections.title: The grammar of shots: a closer look
sections.body:
Film has a grammar. Shots are the words, cuts are the punctuation, and angles and movement are the tone of voice.

SHOT SIZES. A wide (or establishing) shot shows a whole place, so we know where we are. A medium shot shows a person from the waist up, good for conversation. A close-up fills the frame with a face or a detail, so we feel emotion. An extreme close-up pushes to an eye or a shaking hand, for maximum tension.

ANGLES. Eye-level feels natural. A high angle looks down and makes a subject feel small or vulnerable. A low angle looks up and makes them feel powerful. A tilted (Dutch) angle makes a moment feel wrong.

MOVEMENT. A still camera feels calm. A pan or tilt follows action. A dolly or tracking shot glides and feels cinematic. A handheld camera shakes slightly and feels raw and real.

CUTS. A cut is the join between two shots. Most are invisible on purpose. A cut on action hides the edit inside a movement. Cross-cutting jumps between two places to build suspense.

You do not need to memorize these like a test. You need to recognize them, because once you can name a choice, you can make it on purpose.

sections.title: Worked example: how to read one scene
sections.body:
Here is the method in action, so you can copy the shape of the thinking. This is a model, not a film you must watch.

Imagine a chase down a narrow alley. Watch three choices work together:

FIRST, the cuts get shorter and shorter, until each lasts less than a second. CHOICE: fast cutting. EFFECT: your heartbeat climbs.

SECOND, the camera is handheld, right behind the runner. We are inside the fear, not watching calmly. CHOICE: handheld. EFFECT: we feel unsafe too.

THIRD, at the dead end the camera drops to a low angle looking up at the wall, so it towers over us. CHOICE: low angle. EFFECT: the obstacle feels impossible.

Notice the shape: name the choice, then name the feeling. Never just say 'it was exciting.' Say WHAT the filmmaker did and WHAT it did to you. That is a critique.

sections.title: Guided practice: the freeze-frame hunt
sections.body:
Try it before the graded activity. Open any film or show you can watch legally at home.

1. Pause on three different frames that catch your eye.
2. For each, write the shot size (wide, medium, close-up, extreme), the angle (eye-level, high, low), and whether the camera was still or moving.
3. In one sentence per frame, say what that choice made you feel.

This is practice, not graded, and you do not submit it. It warms up the exact muscle you use below.

sections.title: Reflection before your activity
sections.body:
Answer these for yourself before you write your activity. You do not submit them.

- Which tool (shot size, angle, movement, or cuts) do you now notice most easily?
- Which one is still hard to spot?
- In the scene you thought about at the start, can you name one craft choice and the feeling it created?

title: Genre in One Pass
lesson_goal: I want you to recognize film genres from how a film looks and sounds, not just from its story, so you know the rules you will later break.
before_hook: Genre is a promise. When a film opens dark and quiet, you brace for horror. When it opens bright with bouncy music, you expect comedy or romance. You already read these signals without thinking. Today I want to make that skill conscious, because a filmmaker who knows the rules of a genre can play with them, honor them, or break them on purpose.
watch_for: What signals tell you the genre in the first minute?
What does each genre promise the audience?
Which genre would you most want to make, and why?

rubric.criteria: Explains genre from look and sound

sections.title: Warm up: the 30-second guess
sections.body: Think of the last time you knew a film's genre within thirty seconds, before anything happened in the plot. How did you know? Your eyes and ears read the signals for you. Today you make that skill conscious.

sections.title: How genre speaks before the story does
sections.body:
Genre is a promise the audience already understands. A film keeps or breaks that promise, but first it has to make it, and it makes it through look and sound long before the story explains anything.

COLOR tells you mood. Warm golds and soft light promise romance or comedy. Cold blues and heavy shadow promise horror, crime, or thriller.

MUSIC AND SOUND set the pulse. Bouncy, bright music promises fun. Low drones and silence-then-shock promise fear. A swelling orchestra promises adventure or epic.

PACE tells you the kind of ride. Fast cutting and quick scenes promise action or comedy. Slow, held shots promise drama or art film.

SETTING AND COSTUME place the world: neon city, dusty barrio, spaceship, school hallway.

Common genres and their promises: horror (dread, threat), comedy (a light tone and a happy release), romance (two people, a love to win), action (spectacle and stakes), drama (real feeling and change), documentary (this is true).

Why this matters: once you can name the signals, they become tools. A filmmaker who knows the rules can honor them, play with them, or break them on purpose.

sections.title: Worked example: reading the first minute
sections.body:
A model, not a film to watch. Imagine the opening minute of a film with no dialogue yet.

The screen is dim and blue. A single light flickers. The music is a low hum with one high, thin note. The camera holds still for a long time, then a door creaks and we cut fast to a close-up of a wide eye.

Read the signals: cold color (dread), low drone plus a sudden sharp sound (fear), long stillness broken by a fast cut (a scare). Verdict before a word is spoken: this is horror.

Notice the method. You did not use the plot. You named the look and sound signals, then named the promise. That is reading genre like a filmmaker.

sections.title: Guided practice: signal spotting
sections.body:
Open the first two minutes of any film or trailer you can watch legally. With the sound ON:

1. List four signals you notice: one about color, one about music/sound, one about pace, one about setting or costume.
2. From those four signals alone, name the genre you expect.
3. Then keep watching for one more minute. Were you right? If the film surprised you, what signal was misleading on purpose?

Not graded. This trains the eye you will use in the activity.

sections.title: Reflection before your activity
sections.body:
- Which signal do you rely on most: color, sound, pace, or setting?
- Name one film that promised one genre and then broke that promise. What did breaking it make you feel?
- Which genre would you most want to make, and what is its main promise to the audience?

title: Seeing Like a Filipino Filmmaker
lesson_goal: I want you to study one Filipino film or short and take one technique you can use in your own work, so you build a local reference library instead of memorizing trivia.
before_hook: Filipino filmmakers have solved hard problems with small budgets for decades. That is a treasure chest for you. Today I do not want you to memorize names and dates. I want you to watch one Filipino work, see how one moment was built, and steal that technique for yourself. That is how real craft grows.
watch_for: What is one thing this filmmaker did that you could copy?
How did they use a small space, a real location, or natural light?
What feeling did they create, and with what tool?

activity_brief: I want you to name one technique from the film we watched, describe it in 3 to 4 sentences, and say exactly how you would use it in your own future film. Be specific. Do not say the lighting was nice. Say how the filmmaker used a single window as their only light source, and how you would try the same in your own home.

rubric.criteria: Plans a personal use for it

sections.title: Warm up: a technique you admired
sections.body: Think of one Filipino film, short, or teleserye moment that stayed with you. Not the whole story, just one moment that was built well. Today you learn to see how such a moment is made, and to steal the technique for your own work.

sections.title: Big craft on a small budget
sections.body:
Filipino filmmakers have made powerful work with very little money for decades. That is a treasure chest for you, because limits force clever choices, and clever choices are exactly what you can copy.

NATURAL LIGHT. A single window, a doorway, or a bare bulb can light a whole scene for free, and it often looks more honest than expensive equipment. Watch where the light comes from and what it hides.

REAL LOCATIONS. A real house, a real market, a real jeepney gives a scene a truth a built set cannot fake, at almost no cost. The place becomes a character.

THE HUMAN FACE. When you cannot afford spectacle, you point the camera at a face and hold. A close-up on a real expression is the cheapest and strongest shot there is.

SOUND AND SILENCE. Everyday sound, or the sudden absence of it, sets mood without a music budget.

THE LONG TAKE. Holding one shot without cutting makes a moment feel real and continuous, and it costs nothing but courage.

The lesson is not to memorize titles. It is to watch one work closely, see how one moment was built, and carry that one technique into your own films.

sections.title: Worked example: the one-window scene
sections.body:
A model of how to study a technique. Imagine a quiet scene shot in a small room with only the light from one window.

What the filmmaker did: they placed the actor so the window light falls on half the face and leaves the other half in shadow. No lamps, no crew, just the window. The split of light and dark makes the character look caught between two feelings.

How you would copy it: at home, near a window in the afternoon, sit so the light hits one side of your face. Film on a phone. Move closer or further from the window to make the shadow softer or harder. You have just used a National-Artist-level technique for free.

That is the whole game: name the technique, understand why it works, plan how you will use it.

sections.title: Guided practice: plan one shot at home
sections.body:
You will not film for a grade here, just plan.

1. Pick one technique from the reading (natural light, real location, the held face, sound/silence, or the long take).
2. Describe, in 4 to 5 sentences, one shot you could film in your own home or barangay using it: where the camera goes, where the light comes from, what we see.
3. Say what feeling you want that shot to create.

Keep this plan. It feeds straight into your activity.

sections.title: Reflection before your activity
sections.body:
- Which technique feels most possible for you to try with just a phone?
- What is one thing a small budget can do BETTER than a big one?
- Whose work (a Filipino filmmaker, or anyone) would you most like to study next, and why?

title: The Critique
lesson_goal: I want you to write a real film critique: a clear verdict backed by craft evidence, drafted alone, sharpened against an agent, then revised into your best work.
before_hook: This is your first real output. A film critique is not a summary. It is you, using the eye you built over three weeks, judging how a film was made and whether it works. Film schools and employers respect a person who can watch closely and argue clearly. That skill starts here.
watch_for: What is the film trying to do?
Which craft choices help it, and which hurt it?
What is my honest verdict, and can I defend it?

video_candidate: Editors of a leading film magazine explain how a review is built. Reputable and clean.
video_preview_note: Optional lesson. Preview before embedding to confirm the runtime fits.
video_status: SELECTED. Optional. Preview to confirm runtime.

video_runtime: Not confirmed to the second. BFI Behind the scenes clips run short.
after_bridge: So a critique is an argument backed by craft evidence. You make a claim about the film, then you prove it with what you saw on screen. That is the same skill a lawyer, a scientist, and a filmmaker all share. You state a position and you back it.
activity_brief: I want you to choose one short film or one full length film. Write a critique of 300 to 400 words. Make a clear verdict and back it with at least three craft choices you noticed. First write your own draft with no help at all. Then use a free AI agent as a sparring partner: paste your draft and ask it to attack your weakest argument. Read what it says. Keep what is fair. Reject what is wrong. Then revise. Submit a link to a document that shows both your first draft and your final version, so I can see how your thinking grew.
tool: A free writing tool like Google Docs for the document and the shareable link. A free AI chat agent for the sparring step, run through my teacher account or as a class demo, since these tools have age rules for minors. I will confirm the exact agent and its rules in Research mode.
ai_note: You write first, alone. The agent only challenges your draft. You decide what to keep. The argument stays yours. An agent that writes your critique for you has robbed you of the one skill this whole term is building.

rubric.criteria: Three or more craft choices as evidence
Meets length and submits both drafts

sections.title: Warm up: 'I liked it' is not a critique
sections.body: Everyone can say 'I liked it' or 'it was boring.' A critique is different: it is an argument. It makes a clear claim about how a film was made and whether it works, and it backs that claim with what you actually saw on screen. This task is where you learn to argue like that.

sections.title: The anatomy of a critique
sections.body:
A film critique has a shape you can rely on.

THE VERDICT (your claim). One clear sentence: does the film work, and why, in craft terms? Not 'it was good' but 'the film earns its scares through sound and patience, even when its story is thin.' A reader should know your position immediately.

THE EVIDENCE (your proof). At least three specific craft choices you noticed: a shot, a cut, a use of light or music, a performance beat. For each, name the choice and the effect. Vague praise is not evidence. 'The lighting was nice' proves nothing. 'The single overhead light turned the kitchen into a cage' proves something.

THE STRUCTURE. Open with your verdict. Spend the middle proving it, one craft choice per paragraph. Close by returning to the verdict, now earned.

HONEST TONE. A critique can admire and object at the same time. The best ones do both. You are not a hater or a fan, you are a judge.

AND THE AGENT. When you use a free AI agent as a sparring partner, it only attacks your weakest argument so you can make it stronger. It never writes the critique. The argument stays yours, because arguing is the exact skill this task builds.

sections.title: Worked example: a model paragraph
sections.body:
Here is one body paragraph doing its job. Read how the claim, evidence, and effect lock together.

'The film's fear lives in its sound, not its monster. For most of the second act we never see the creature; we only hear it, a low wet breathing that the sound mix pushes just under the music. Because the threat stays off screen, our own imagination builds something worse than any costume could. The one time the film shows the creature in full, the tension actually drops. That single choice, to hide and only hint, is why the film works.'

Notice: a claim (fear lives in sound), specific evidence (off-screen breathing under the music), and the effect (imagination does the work), then an honest observation that showing the monster weakens it. That is a critique in miniature.

sections.title: Guided practice: outline before you write
sections.body:
Do this before your full activity. Choose the film you will critique, then write only an outline:

1. Your VERDICT in one sentence.
2. Three craft choices you will use as evidence (one line each: the choice, and the effect).
3. One honest weakness you will admit.

A critique with a strong outline almost writes itself. Keep this; it becomes the skeleton of your submission.

sections.title: Reflection before your activity
sections.body:
- Is your verdict something a reasonable person could disagree with? (A real claim can be argued.)
- Which of your three pieces of evidence is strongest? Which is weakest?
- When the AI agent attacks your weakest point, what is your plan: defend it better, or cut it?

title: Story Structure, the Spine
lesson_goal: I want you to see the shape under every story, the hook, the rising stakes, and the payoff, and to break a story you know into those three parts.
before_hook: Every story you remember has a shape. A beginning that pulls you in. A middle that raises the stakes. An end that pays off. That shape is structure, and it is the spine of every screenplay ever written. Without it, a story just wanders and the audience drifts away. Today I want you to feel that spine, because once you feel it, you can build any story on it.
watch_for: Where does this story hook you?
How do the stakes rise in the middle?
How does the ending pay off the beginning?

after_bridge: So structure is the spine that holds a story upright. Hook, rising stakes, payoff. Beginning, middle, end. It sounds simple, and it is, but almost every weak story fails right here. Master this shape and you are ahead of most beginners.
activity_brief: I want you to take any story you know well, a film or a folk tale, and break it into beginning, middle, and end in 5 to 7 sentences. Name the hook that pulls you in, the rising stakes in the middle, and the payoff at the end. Show me you can see the spine.

sections.title: Warm up: the story you cannot forget
sections.body: Bring to mind one story you will never forget, from any film, book, or folk tale. It stuck because it had a shape: it pulled you in, raised the stakes, and paid off. That shape is structure, and today you learn to see its spine.

sections.title: The three-act spine
sections.body:
Almost every story that works rests on the same spine: a beginning that hooks you, a middle that raises the stakes, and an end that pays off. Screenwriters call these the three acts.

ACT ONE: SETUP. We meet the character and their ordinary world, then something breaks the routine, the inciting incident, and the story truly begins. The hook lives here: the question that makes us need to know what happens.

ACT TWO: CONFRONTATION. The character chases what they want and keeps hitting walls. Stakes rise. Around the middle comes a midpoint, a twist or a point of no return that changes the direction and raises the pressure. This act is the longest and where most weak stories sag.

ACT THREE: RESOLUTION. Everything builds to a climax, the biggest confrontation, then a resolution that answers the hook from Act One. A good payoff feels surprising yet, looking back, inevitable.

HOOK AND PAYOFF are a pair. Whatever question you raise at the start, you must answer at the end. When a story wanders and loses you, it is almost always because the spine is missing: no clear hook, flat stakes, or a payoff that ignores the beginning.

sections.title: Worked example: mapping a familiar tale
sections.body:
A model using the shape of a simple tale, so you can copy the method.

SETUP: a poor young fisher lives an ordinary life by the sea (ordinary world). One day the net pulls up a talking fish that offers one wish (inciting incident). HOOK: what will they wish for, and what will it cost?

CONFRONTATION: the fisher wishes for wealth, gets it, and wants more. Each new wish brings a new problem. MIDPOINT: the wishes start taking more than they give, and the fisher cannot stop.

RESOLUTION: the final wish costs the fisher the one thing that mattered. CLIMAX and payoff: the sea takes everything back, answering the opening question, they wanted more than they needed, and lost what they had.

Notice the method: name the three acts, find the inciting incident, the midpoint, and the way the ending answers the hook. That is reading structure.

sections.title: Guided practice: break a story into three acts
sections.body:
Pick any story you know well, a film or a folk tale.

1. Write its SETUP in one or two sentences, and name the inciting incident.
2. Write the CONFRONTATION: what does the character want, what blocks them, and what is the midpoint twist?
3. Write the RESOLUTION: the climax and how it pays off the hook.

Not graded. This is the exact move your activity asks for, done once as practice.

sections.title: Reflection before your activity
sections.body:
- In your chosen story, what is the single question the hook plants in your mind?
- Does the ending answer that exact question? If not, the spine has a crack, where?
- Which act do you find hardest to build in your own ideas: the setup, the middle, or the payoff?

title: Character and Want, the Engine
lesson_goal: I want you to build a character the audience cares about by giving them a clear want and a real obstacle.
before_hook: A story moves because someone wants something and cannot easily get it. That want is the engine. A character with no clear want is a character no one cares about. Your strongest ideas often come from found stories, real moments from your own life that you reshape into fiction. Today you build a character with a beating heart.
watch_for: What does the main character want?
What stands in their way?
How does the want drive every choice they make?

after_bridge: So character is the engine and want is the fuel. Give a character a clear want and a real obstacle, and your story almost writes itself, because every scene becomes the character trying to get what they want and hitting a wall. That is drama.
activity_brief: I want you to invent one character in 5 to 7 sentences. Name what they want, what blocks them, and why the audience should care. You can base them on a real person you reshape into fiction. Make the want specific. Do not say they want to be happy. Say they want to win the barangay basketball trophy their late father never won.

sections.title: Warm up: the character you rooted for
sections.body: Think of a character you desperately wanted to succeed. Why did you care? Almost always it is because they wanted something badly and something stood in their way. That engine, want plus obstacle, is what today is about.

sections.title: Want, obstacle, and stakes
sections.body:
A story moves because someone wants something and cannot easily get it. Remove the want and the story stops.

THE WANT must be specific. 'To be happy' is not a want; it is a fog. 'To win the barangay basketball trophy her late father never won' is a want, because we can see it, and we can see her fail or succeed at it.

EXTERNAL vs INTERNAL. The external want is the visible goal (win the trophy, get the role, reach home). The internal want is the deeper need (to feel worthy, to be forgiven, to belong). The strongest characters chase both, and the two often pull against each other.

THE OBSTACLE is what stands in the way: another person, a rule, the world, or the character's own fear. Without an obstacle the want is granted instantly and there is no story.

STAKES answer 'so what?' They are what the character loses if they fail. High, personal stakes are why we lean forward.

FOUND STORIES. Your strongest characters often start from real life, a real person or moment you reshape into fiction. You keep the truth of the feeling and change the facts.

Give a character a clear want and a real obstacle and your story almost writes itself: every scene becomes them trying to get it and hitting a wall.

sections.title: Worked example: building a wanting character
sections.body:
A model. Watch a flat idea become a character.

FLAT: 'A boy who likes to draw.' No want, no obstacle, nothing to care about.

ADD A SPECIFIC WANT: 'A boy who wants to win the regional comics contest so his name is printed in the paper his lola reads.'

ADD AN OBSTACLE: 'But he has to share the family's one phone, which his sister needs for online class, so he can only draw at midnight.'

ADD INTERNAL STAKES: 'He believes that if his lola sees his name in print, she will finally believe art is not a waste of time.'

Now every scene has fuel: stolen midnight hours, the sister's deadline, the fear of not being taken seriously. Same boy, but now we care, because the want is specific, the obstacle is real, and the stakes are personal.

sections.title: Guided practice: the character sketch
sections.body:
Invent one character in a short sketch (this is practice for your activity):

1. Name their specific external want (something we could see them win or lose).
2. Name one real obstacle in the way.
3. Name the internal stakes: why it matters to them personally.
4. Base any part of it on a real person or moment you reshape.

Keep it. It becomes the seed of your submission.

sections.title: Reflection before your activity
sections.body:
- Is your character's want specific enough that we could watch them fail at it?
- Does the obstacle come from outside, from inside the character, or both?
- What real feeling from your own life did you reshape into this character?

title: Owning Your Voice
lesson_goal: I want you to understand why your own voice is your value, and to set your own honest rule for using an AI agent in your writing.
before_hook: Anyone can now generate a script with one click. That is exactly why your own voice is worth more than ever. Originality is not just about honesty. It is your career edge. A writer whose voice is provably their own is the one who gets hired. Plagiarism and lazy agent use throw that edge away. Today you decide what kind of writer you will be.
watch_for: What makes a writer's voice their own?
Where is the line between inspiration and copying?
How can an agent help you without stealing your voice?

after_bridge: So your voice is your value. Use an agent as a tool that serves your voice, never as a replacement for it. The writer who owns their voice owns their future. The one who lets a machine write for them has nothing to sell that a machine cannot already give away for free.
activity_brief: I want you to write 5 to 7 sentences on what makes your writing voice yours. Think about how you see the world, the stories only you could tell, the way you use words. Then state one clear rule you will follow for using an AI agent honestly in your own screenwriting this term.
tool: None needed. This lesson is about AI ethics itself, so you write it in your own words with no agent.

sections.title: Warm up: what makes your voice yours
sections.body: Anyone can now generate a script with one click. That is exactly why your own voice is worth more than ever, not less. Today you decide what kind of writer you will be, and you set your own honest rule for using an AI agent.

sections.title: Voice, plagiarism, and honest AI use
sections.body:
YOUR VOICE is the way only you see and say things: the stories only you could tell, the rhythm of your sentences, the details you notice. It is your value as a writer, and it is the one thing a machine cannot give away for free.

PLAGIARISM is passing off someone else's work as your own. It comes in forms worth naming. Copying is the obvious one. PATCHWRITING is sneakier: taking someone's sentences and swapping a few words so it 'looks' original. AI PLAGIARISM is letting an agent write the work and submitting it as yours. All three throw away the one thing that makes you hireable, a voice that is provably yours.

HONEST AI USE keeps the agent as a tool that serves your voice, never as the author. Good uses: ask it to challenge your weakest argument, to point out where your dialogue sounds fake, to quiz you, to explain a concept. Bad uses: ask it to write the scene, then hand that in.

A SIMPLE TEST: after the agent helps, is the work still unmistakably yours? Could you defend every line as your own thinking? If yes, you used it honestly. If the machine did the thinking, you robbed yourself of the skill this whole term is building.

CULTURAL RESPECT matters too. Drawing from a culture that is not yours without care or credit is its own kind of taking. Write from what you know, and when you borrow, honor the source.

sections.title: Worked example: two ways to use an agent
sections.body:
A model showing the line between honest and dishonest use, on the same task: writing a short scene.

VOICE-STEALING: The student types 'write me a two-page scene about a fisherman and his son' and submits what comes back. The words are fluent, but none of them are the student's. There is nothing to defend, nothing learned, and nothing only this student could have made.

VOICE-SERVING: The student writes the scene themselves, from a real memory of their own lolo. Then they paste it to the agent and ask, 'Which line of dialogue sounds least like a real person?' The agent flags one stiff line. The student rewrites it in their own words. The scene is still theirs, only sharper.

Same tool, opposite outcomes. The difference is who does the thinking.

sections.title: Guided practice: draft your AI rule
sections.body:
Write your own honest rule for using an AI agent in your screenwriting this term. Make it specific enough to follow. Answer these in your rule:

1. What WILL you let an agent do for you? (e.g., challenge, quiz, explain)
2. What will you NEVER let it do?
3. How will you make sure the final work is still provably your voice?

This rule is the heart of your activity, and you will follow it for the rest of the term.

sections.title: Reflection before your activity
sections.body:
- Describe your writing voice in one honest sentence. What do only you notice?
- Have you ever been tempted to patchwrite or let a machine do the work? What did it cost, or nearly cost?
- Read your AI rule aloud. Could you follow it even on a night you are tired and behind?

sections.title: Warm up: the uniform that gets you read
sections.body: A brilliant story in the wrong format gets thrown out unread in the real world. Format is the uniform of a professional writer: follow it and a reader takes you seriously before they read a single line. The good news is a free tool puts the uniform on for you.

sections.title: How a screenplay page is built
sections.body:
Screenplay format is a shared standard so anyone can read your pages instantly. Learn these five elements.

SCENE HEADING (slugline). All caps, tells us three things: interior or exterior, the place, and the time. Example: INT. CLASSROOM - DAY. It orients the reader before the scene starts.

ACTION LINES. Written in the present tense, describing only what we can see and hear. Not thoughts, not backstory. 'Maria drops her bag and freezes.' Keep them lean.

CHARACTER NAME. In capitals and centered above the character's dialogue, so we know who speaks.

DIALOGUE. Sits under the character name, what they actually say.

PARENTHETICAL. A short cue in brackets under the name for how a line is said, used sparingly. (whispering)

A free tool like WriterDuet, Celtx, or even a screenplay template handles the margins, the capitals, and the centering automatically, so you focus on the story while the tool wears the uniform for you.

Why it matters: correct format signals you are serious, and it makes your pages readable at a glance. Wrong format signals the opposite, and busy readers stop.

sections.title: Worked example: a correctly formatted scene
sections.body:
A model of the format. Read how each element sits.

INT. SARI-SARI STORE - NIGHT

Rain hammers the tin roof. ALDO (16), soaked, counts coins on the counter.

ALDO
(quietly)
Two more. I just need two more.

The SHOPKEEPER slides a candle across the counter, then pushes the coins back.

SHOPKEEPER
Pay me when the lights come back.

Notice: the heading tells us where and when in caps; the action is present tense and only shows what we see and hear; names are centered and capitalized; a parenthetical gives one small cue. That is the whole uniform. Now the reader trusts you.

sections.title: Guided practice: format a tiny scene
sections.body:
Before your activity, format a very short scene by hand or in a free tool:

1. Write one scene heading (INT. or EXT., a place, a time).
2. Write two action lines in the present tense.
3. Write one character name (capitalized, centered) with two lines of dialogue.

Do not worry about a great story here, worry about clean, correct format. This is the exact skill your submission is graded on.

sections.title: Reflection before your activity
sections.body:
- Which element is easiest to get wrong: the heading, the action tense, or the dialogue layout?
- Which free tool will you use, and have you opened it yet?
- Why do you think professionals are so strict about format?

sections.title: Warm up: a piece you can show the world
sections.body: This is your output for the term. A short, tight, well-formatted screenplay that you wrote yourself is a real portfolio piece, something you could send to a workshop, a contest, or a school. Most people your age have never finished one. You are about to.

sections.title: Bringing it all together
sections.body:
This task pulls in everything you have learned. A short screenplay that works stands on four legs.

STRUCTURE. Even in two to four pages, give it a spine: a hook that opens a question, rising stakes in the middle, and a payoff that answers the hook. Short does not mean shapeless.

CHARACTER. Someone wants something specific and hits a real obstacle. In a short script you have no room for a character who wants nothing.

FORMAT. Correct scene headings, present-tense action, centered names, clean dialogue. The uniform you learned last task.

VOICE. This is yours. Follow the honest AI rule you wrote in Task 3.

AND ONE MORE THING, PERFORMABLE DIALOGUE. Dialogue is not how people write, it is how people talk. The test is simple: read it aloud. If it sounds stiff or speech-like, it fails. If it sounds like a real person in a real moment, it works. This is the one thing you will ask a free AI agent to test, and only this: does the dialogue sound performable when read aloud? You keep the notes that help and reject the rest. You decide. The screenplay stays yours.

FINALLY, REVISION. First drafts are where you find the story; revision is where the writing actually gets good. Outline, draft, test, revise. Submit all three so your growth is visible.

sections.title: Worked example: dialogue that reads aloud
sections.body:
A model of the performable-dialogue test on two versions of the same line.

STIFF (fails the read-aloud test):
BEN
I am very angry with you because you did not tell me that our mother was sick and now I feel betrayed.

No one talks like that. It is information, not speech.

PERFORMABLE (passes):
BEN
You knew. You knew about Nanay and you let me find out from a neighbor.
(beat)
I'm not even angry. That's the problem.

Same situation, but now it sounds like a real person: shorter, sharper, with something left unsaid. That is what the read-aloud test catches, and it is the only thing you will ask the agent to check.

sections.title: Guided practice: outline your screenplay
sections.body:
Before you draft, outline (this is the first thing you submit):

1. Your HOOK: the question the opening plants.
2. Your CHARACTER's specific want and the obstacle.
3. The MIDDLE: how the stakes rise.
4. Your PAYOFF: how the ending answers the hook.
5. One line of dialogue you already know a character will say.

A screenplay built on a clear outline is far easier to write and revise.

sections.title: Reflection before your activity
sections.body:
- Does your two-to-four-page story have a real hook and a real payoff, or does it just stop?
- Read one line of your planned dialogue aloud now. Does it sound like a person?
- What will you ask the AI agent to test, and what will you refuse to let it do?
